name: Protein: the body's repair-and-build crew
strand: Macros: why your body needs them
scope: Protein is the body's building AND working material — the 'grow-and-fix' macro, revealed one job at a time. T1: the reason a plate pairs meat/eggs/fish as the 'building' food is that your body patches a scraped knee and grows new muscle out of PROTEIN. T2: the stringy fibers you pull apart in a chicken breast literally ARE bundled muscle protein — eating meat means eating another animal's muscle. T3: hair and fingernails are a tough protein (keratin) too — another reason 'eat your protein' isn't only about muscle. T4: protein isn't just structure — the spit that makes a plain cracker taste sweeter the longer you chew is doing it with an ENZYME, and every enzyme is a protein (your digestion tools are protein). T5: the antibodies that fight off a cold are proteins as well, which is why a sick kid still needs to eat (broth, eggs) to rebuild defenses. T5: your body takes the protein in a steak APART into ~20 small pieces called amino acids and restrings those same 'beads' into YOUR proteins. T5: nine of those amino-acid beads your body cannot make at all — 'essential' on a nutrition label means 'must arrive in food.' T8 (payoff): hemoglobin, the stuff that makes blood red and carries your oxygen, is a protein cradle built around an iron atom — so a beef steak helps build the very blood in your veins. Also seeds: protein keeps you full far longer than a sugary cereal (satiety); a burn or wound heals by laying down new protein.
source: Established textbook nutrition/biochemistry (protein as structural + functional macro; ~20 amino acids, 9 essential for humans; enzymes and antibodies are proteins; hemoglobin = globin protein + heme iron). Corroborated in passing via the complementary-protein searches (Wikipedia 'Protein combining', 'Diet for a Small Planet'). Grokipedia 'Protein'/'Essential amino acid' attempted but WebFetch returned HTTP 403 this session — flag for build-stage cross-check against Grokipedia + Wikipedia 'Protein (nutrient)', 'Essential amino acid', 'Hemoglobin'.
framing_note: Empowerment voice: a kid learns WHY the plate needs a protein. Scene-led (a scraped knee, a chewed cracker, a cold), never 'What is protein?'. ONE job per rung — muscle, keratin, enzymes, antibodies, amino-acid recycling, 'essential', blood are SEVEN different payoffs, not restatements of each other. Accuracy rail: nine essential amino acids for humans (do NOT say 'all 20 must come from food'); amino acids are the tested CONCEPT ('beads'), never their chemical/Latin names as the answer. Dinner-test payoff = the hemoglobin / steak-builds-your-blood rung.

name: The complete protein: all nine blocks in one bite
strand: Macros: why your body needs them
scope: Why nutritionists call some foods 'complete' proteins, built scene-first. T1: 'complete' means a food carries ALL nine essential amino acids in usable amounts at once — and the foods that pull that off are the animal ones: meat, fish, eggs, milk. T2: most single plant foods are 'incomplete' — a bowl of plain rice is short on one bead (lysine), a scoop of beans short on another (methionine) — so no one of them covers all nine alone. T3 (payoff): the EGG is the protein gold standard — scientists literally score every other protein against egg white, because an egg has to hold everything needed to build a whole chick from scratch. T4: milk actually hides two proteins with different speeds — the curds (casein) digest slow, the watery whey fast, which is why 'whey' is the athlete's shake and casein the 'overnight' one. T5: soy and quinoa are the rare PLANT foods complete on their own — the exceptions that prove the rule.
source: Search: complementary/complete protein (Wikipedia 'Protein combining'; 'Diet for a Small Planet'; Forks Over Knives 'Myth of Complementary Protein'). Egg biological-value 'reference protein' and casein/whey digestion speeds are established food-science facts (recommend Grokipedia/Wikipedia 'Egg white', 'Biological value', 'Whey protein' cross-check at build). Grokipedia WebFetch 403 this session.
framing_note: Invert the wonder: put 'the food scientists measure every other protein against' in the STEM, make the knowable EGG the answer. Scene-led, never 'What is a complete protein?'. Keep all four choices live (other complete animal foods as distractors, not obvious wrongs). Accuracy rail: NINE essential amino acids; egg is the reference protein — teach the CONCEPT 'gold-standard/reference protein', never a memorized biological-value number as the answer. Traditional-foods lean is gentle (animal foods happen to be complete) but the tested FACTS are settled, so not vision-mandated. Dinner-test payoff = the egg-is-the-reference rung.

name: Red meat's hidden payload: heme iron & B12
strand: Macros: why your body needs them
scope: Beyond protein, red meat carries two things plants barely provide — the honest empowerment case for a growing kid. T1: red meat is loaded with iron, the mineral your blood needs to carry oxygen — the reason liver and red meat are the classic 'build-your-blood' foods. T2 (payoff): meat's iron is the 'heme' kind, tucked inside the same molecule that makes blood red, and your gut grabs it far more readily than the iron in spinach — Popeye's spinach iron is REAL iron, but the body absorbs only a small fraction of it. T3: a squeeze of lemon or a sliced tomato (vitamin C) at the meal boosts how much of the PLANT iron you actually absorb — a real cooking trick. T4: vitamin B12 — needed to build blood and nerves — is found almost ONLY in animal foods (meat, eggs, dairy, fish); it's the nutrient strict vegans must take as a supplement. T5: this is why traditional cultures prized organ meats and blood dishes (liver, black pudding) — the most nutrient-dense bites per mouthful.
source: Established nutrition (heme vs non-heme iron bioavailability; vitamin C enhances non-heme absorption; B12 essentially only in animal foods — the classic vegan-supplement fact). Recommend build-stage Grokipedia/Wikipedia cross-check: 'Heme iron', 'Human iron metabolism', 'Vitamin B12'. Grokipedia WebFetch 403 this session; not separately web-verified beyond established consensus.
framing_note: Empowerment, not moralizing: a kid learns WHY meat is nutritionally valuable. STEEL-MAN both sides at build — mainstream 'limit red meat' guidance is real and honest; the iron+B12 case is the traditional-foods counter. Do not strawman either camp. Scene-led (a steak, Popeye's spinach, a wedge of lemon on the plate). Accuracy rail: heme vs non-heme is about ABSORPTION (bioavailability), not that plant iron is 'fake'; vitamin C boosting non-heme iron is well established. Teach concepts, never mg figures as the answer. VISION-MANDATED: 'red meat is uniquely valuable' is a culturally contested stance. Dinner-test payoff = the heme-iron / Popeye rung.

name: Why a growing kid and an athlete need more protein
strand: Macros: why your body needs them
scope: Protein need isn't one-size-fits-all — bodies that are BUILDING need more. T1: a growing kid is literally adding new body every year — bone, muscle, organs, all built from protein — so per pound of bodyweight a kid needs more than a sedentary grown-up. T2: lifting weights or hard training TEARS tiny bits of muscle; it grows back bigger only if protein is on hand to rebuild it — the 'eat protein after training' rule. T3 (payoff): among the amino-acid beads, one called leucine (rich in eggs, meat, dairy) acts as the 'GO' signal that switches muscle-building on — which is why athletes chase protein at breakfast, not just at dinner. T4: pregnant and nursing mothers need extra protein because they're building a whole second person. T5: the deficiency picture — kwashiorkor, the swollen-belly malnutrition seen when a just-weaned toddler is filled up on starchy porridge but given almost no protein; the name is a Ghanaian (Ga) word for 'the sickness the older child gets when the new baby comes.'
source: Search: kwashiorkor (Wikipedia 'Kwashiorkor'; ScienceDirect overview; ResearchGate 'The Story of Kwashiorkor') confirming protein-deficiency-with-adequate-calories, Ga-language etymology 'deposed/displaced child', first described by Cicely Williams (1933, Gold Coast). Growth/athlete protein need and leucine as MPS trigger are established sports-nutrition facts (build-stage cross-check: Grokipedia/Wikipedia 'Leucine', 'Muscle protein synthesis').
framing_note: Voice: honest and empowering — enough CALORIES is not the same as enough PROTEIN (that's the kwashiorkor lesson, and why the belly swells even when the child is 'fed'). Scene-led (a growing kid outgrowing shoes, post-workout, a bowl of porridge). Accuracy rail: kwashiorkor = protein deficiency WITH roughly adequate calories; Ga-language Ghanaian etymology; teach it as the vivid concept, never as a tested medical term or the discoverer's name as the answer. Leucine = 'the go-signal bead', concept not chemistry. Dinner-test payoff = the leucine / protein-timing rung.

name: Collagen & gelatin: the protein in bone broth
strand: Macros: why your body needs them
scope: The most abundant protein in your body is a stringy 'glue' called collagen — and it's the same stuff that makes a great broth wobble. T1: the tough, chewy connective tissue in a cheap cut, and the gristle around a joint, is collagen — the body's built-in glue and scaffolding for skin, tendon, and bone. T2 (payoff): simmer bones and tough cuts low-and-slow for hours and the collagen melts into gelatin — the reason a proper stock or bone broth sets to a jiggly jelly in the fridge, and the reason cheap tough cuts (shank, oxtail) turn meltingly tender when braised. T3: that same gelatin, purified, is what sets a wobbling jelly, a gummy candy, and panna cotta — a dessert built, surprisingly, from animal collagen.
source: Established food science (collagen = most abundant body protein, connective tissue; heat converts collagen to gelatin, giving stock its set and braises their tenderness; gelatin sets jelly/gummies/panna cotta). Build-stage cross-check: Grokipedia/Wikipedia 'Collagen', 'Gelatin', 'Stock (food)'. Grokipedia WebFetch 403 this session.
framing_note: Prep-frame welcome (you simmer, you braise). Reveal the MECHANISM: long slow heat converts collagen -> gelatin (tough becomes tender + the broth jiggles). Scene-led (a stock that wobbles cold, a gummy bear), never 'What is collagen?'. Accuracy rail: gelatin is DENATURED collagen from animal connective tissue — keep it matter-of-fact for a kid (it comes from skin/bone/gristle), never gory; do NOT claim eating collagen rebuilds your own collagen (that's contested marketing) — the tested facts are the COOKING transformation and the dessert set. Dinner-test payoff = the broth-turns-to-jelly rung.

name: Fat is not the enemy: what fat actually does
strand: Macros: why your body needs them
scope: Fat spent decades cast as the diet villain, but it does jobs no other macro can. T1: fat is the body's densest fuel — gram for gram it packs more than double the energy of sugar or protein, which is why a single spoon of oil is so calorie-rich and why body fat is our long-term battery. T2: every one of your cells is wrapped in a wall built of fat (the membrane) — no dietary fat, no cell walls; fat is STRUCTURE, not just fuel. T3: your BRAIN is roughly 60% fat, and the insulation sheathing your nerves is fatty — which is why fat matters most for the youngest, fastest-growing brains (breast milk is deliberately rich in fat for exactly this). T4 (payoff): cholesterol — the word people fear — is the raw material your body turns into hormones (the ones that drive growth and puberty) and into vitamin D from sunlight; you would die without it, and your own liver makes most of it. T5: fat also makes a meal SATISFYING and slows digestion — the reason a fatty meal keeps hunger away for hours while a fat-free snack leaves you hungry soon after. Also seeds: fat under the skin insulates and cushions organs; fat is where much of a dish's FLAVOR lives (fat carries taste and aroma).
source: Established physiology/biochemistry (fat ~9 kcal/g vs ~4 for carb/protein; phospholipid cell membranes; brain ~60% fat by dry weight, myelin is lipid-rich; cholesterol is precursor to steroid hormones + vitamin D + bile, mostly endogenously synthesized; dietary fat slows gastric emptying/increases satiety). Build-stage cross-check: Grokipedia/Wikipedia 'Fat', 'Cholesterol', 'Cell membrane', 'Myelin'. Grokipedia WebFetch 403 this session.
framing_note: STANCE ladder (vision-mandated): steel-man the low-fat orthodoxy honestly (there WERE reasons dietitians pushed low-fat) but LEAN toward 'fat is essential and was over-vilified.' Empowerment: a kid learns what fat DOES. Scene-led (a spoon of oil, the fatty brain, fat-rich breast milk), never 'What is fat?'. ONE job per rung — fuel, membranes, brain, hormones/cholesterol, satiety, flavor are distinct payoffs. Accuracy rail: cholesterol is a precursor to steroid hormones + vitamin D and is mostly liver-made — do not moralize it as 'bad'; energy density taught as 'more than double' carbs/protein, never the exact 9-vs-4 number as the answer. Dinner-test payoff = the cholesterol-makes-hormones rung.

name: Fat carries the vitamins: why you butter your carrots
strand: Macros: why your body needs them
scope: A cooking rule with a hidden reason — some vitamins can't get into you without fat riding shotgun. T1: vitamins A, D, E and K are 'fat-soluble' — they dissolve in fat, not water, so a meal needs some fat present for your body to absorb them at all. T2 (payoff): the orange in a carrot is beta-carotene, which your body converts to vitamin A — but eaten raw and fat-free you absorb little; add butter or oil (glazed carrots, carrots in a stew) and absorption jumps. T3: the same trick powers a salad — a drizzle of olive oil over leafy greens and tomatoes lets you actually absorb their fat-soluble goodness, while a fat-free dressing wastes much of it. T4: it's why traditional cooks paired fat with vegetables on instinct — spinach with butter, tomatoes simmered in olive oil (the red pigment lycopene is absorbed far better cooked in oil). T5: the flip side — fat-soluble vitamins can be BANKED in your body fat for a rainy day (unlike vitamin C, which you must eat daily), so a fat-rich food like egg yolk or cod-liver oil stores up vitamins A and D.
source: Established nutrition (fat-soluble vitamins A/D/E/K require dietary fat for absorption and are stored in body fat; beta-carotene -> vitamin A; carotenoid/lycopene absorption enhanced by fat and by cooking). Build-stage cross-check: Grokipedia/Wikipedia 'Fat-soluble vitamin', 'Beta-Carotene', 'Lycopene'. Grokipedia WebFetch 403 this session.
framing_note: Prep-frame welcome (you butter, you drizzle, you simmer). Reveal the MECHANISM: fat is the CARRIER for A/D/E/K. Invert the wonder — stem sets up 'why grandma always put butter on the carrots', the answer is 'the vitamin needs fat to be absorbed.' Accuracy rail: fat-soluble vitamins are A, D, E, K (NOT C, which is water-soluble); beta-carotene->vitamin A and lycopene are the concrete examples — teach the concept, not the compound names as the tested answer. Dinner-test payoff = the buttered-carrots / beta-carotene rung. Settled science, not vision-mandated.

name: Solid, liquid & spoiling: saturated, mono, poly (and the trans-fat villain)
strand: Macros: why your body needs them
scope: Why some fats are solid at room temperature and some stay liquid — and which one to actually cook in. T1: saturated fats (butter, lard, beef tallow, coconut oil) are SOLID at room temperature because their molecules are straight and stack tight; the pourable oils (olive, seed oils) can't stack. T2: that same tight packing makes saturated fats STABLE under heat — the reason old-school deep-frying used lard/tallow and why coconut oil sits happily on a shelf. T3 (payoff): the delicate polyunsaturated fats in seed oils have 'kinks' that break down and oxidize (go rancid, throw off-flavors and byproducts) when heated hard — the case for searing in a stable fat and saving fragile oils for cold use; olive oil (monounsaturated) sits in the sturdy middle. T4: this shelf-life problem is exactly what food companies 'solved' by hydrogenation — forcing hydrogen into liquid oil to make it solid and shelf-stable, which gave us margarine and, in 1911, Crisco, from cheap vegetable oil. T5: but hydrogenation birthed TRANS fat — the one fat scientists broadly agree is genuinely harmful (it worsens cholesterol both directions), now banned from the US food supply. The irony closer: the engineered fat built to replace 'unhealthy' butter turned out worse than what it replaced.
source: Search: trans fat (PMC8452362 'Demise of Artificial Trans Fat'; FDA PHO final determination pages; Wikipedia 'Trans fat', 'Trans fat regulation') confirming Crisco 1911, hydrogenation makes liquid oil solid/shelf-stable, US ban (GRAS revoked 2015, compliance 2018, final ~2020-2021). Fat structure (saturated stacks tight->solid+stable; PUFA oxidizes on heating; MUFA intermediate) is established lipid chemistry — build-stage cross-check Grokipedia/Wikipedia 'Saturated fat', 'Polyunsaturated fat', 'Hydrogenation'.
framing_note: VISION-MANDATED cooking/seed-oil debate: steel-man the mainstream (polyunsaturated fats lower LDL in trials; seed oils are not proven toxic) but LEAN skeptical of HEATED seed oils and sympathetic to stable traditional fats for high-heat cooking. Reveal the MECHANISM (molecular straightness -> solid + heat-stable). Scene-led (butter vs oil at room temp; a smoking pan). Accuracy rail: Crisco = 1911 (margarine, ~1869, predates it — attribute correctly); trans fat is the SETTLED-harmful one — teach 'the engineered solid fat we banned', not the ban date as the answer. Keep NATURAL saturated fat (contested) distinct from ARTIFICIAL trans fat (settled bad). Dinner-test payoff = the seed-oil-oxidizes-when-heated rung; the trans-fat-irony rung is the closer.

name: Omega-3 vs omega-6: the fish-and-seed-oil balance
strand: Macros: why your body needs them
scope: Two families of fat your body can't make and must eat — and why their BALANCE is argued over. T1: omega-3 and omega-6 are both 'essential' fats (the body cannot build them from scratch); the richest omega-3 comes from OILY FISH — salmon, sardines, mackerel — plus flax and walnuts. T2 (payoff): the most usable omega-3s (the brain-and-heart forms, EPA and DHA) come ready-made in fish and shellfish, while the plant form (in flax/chia/walnut) is a 'starter' your body converts only poorly — which is why 'eat oily fish' beats 'drink flax oil.' T3: omega-6 is everywhere and easy to get — it's the dominant fat in seed/vegetable oils, so anyone eating modern processed food gets plenty (arguably too much). T4: the debate — traditional diets ran roughly balanced between the two families, but modern seed-oil-heavy diets tilt hard toward omega-6; one camp argues this ratio drives inflammation, the mainstream counter argues total omega-3 intake matters more than the ratio. T5: the practical takeaway BOTH sides share — most people are simply short on omega-3, so the fix is more oily fish (or eggs and beef from pastured animals), not obsessing over a number.
source: Search: omega-6/omega-3 (PMC8504498 and PMC7721408 on low omega-6/3 ratio; Eufic 'Do seed oils cause inflammation?' for the mainstream steel-man; thewholehealthpractice 'Seed Oils: Striking the Right Balance') confirming both essential, EPA/DHA (fish) vs ALA (plants) conversion is poor, modern ~10-20:1 omega-6:3 tilt, and the genuine ratio-vs-absolute-intake scientific dispute (incl. Jackson et al. 2024 skepticism of the ratio).
framing_note: VISION-MANDATED contested debate — a flagship 'great nutrition debate' of this strand: present the ratio-matters camp AND the mainstream 'absolute omega-3 is what counts' camp FAIRLY; the shared conclusion (eat more oily fish) is the honest closer, never a strawman of either side. Scene-led (a fillet of salmon; a bottle of vegetable oil). Accuracy rail: both are essential fatty acids; EPA/DHA (fish, ready-made) vs ALA (plants, poorly converted) is the key mechanism — teach 'fish gives the usable kind', never the abbreviations as the tested answer; do NOT overclaim omega-6 is toxic. Dinner-test payoff = the fish-gives-the-usable-omega-3 rung.

name: Carbs are fuel: simple, complex & the glycogen battery
strand: Macros: why your body needs them
scope: Carbohydrates are the body's quick fuel — where they come from, fast vs slow, and how the body stores them. T1: nearly all carbs are built by PLANTS out of sunlight — bread, rice, potato, fruit, and sugar all trace back to a plant storing energy, so carbs are basically edible sunlight. T2: 'simple' carbs (the sugar in candy, juice, honey) are small and hit the blood fast; 'complex' carbs (the starch in bread, rice, potato) are long chains that break down slower — the difference between a sugar rush and steady energy. T3 (payoff): your body's ready fuel is glucose, and your BRAIN is the greediest customer — it runs almost entirely on glucose and burns a big share of your daily carbs just thinking. T4: extra carbs get packed away as GLYCOGEN — a fast-access battery stashed in your liver and muscles; a marathoner 'carb-loads' on a big pasta dinner the night before to top that battery off. T5: run the battery empty and you 'hit the wall' — the sudden mile-20 exhaustion when muscle glycogen runs out and the body scrambles to burn fat instead. Also seeds: fruit's sugar (fructose) is handled mainly by the liver; the body CAN run on fat/ketones when carbs are scarce, so carbs are the DEFAULT fuel, not the only one.
source: Established physiology (glucose is the body's primary ready fuel; brain relies heavily on glucose, ~120 g/day; glycogen stored in liver + muscle; endurance carb-loading and glycogen depletion 'the wall'; fructose primarily hepatic; ketone/fat oxidation as alternative fuel). Build-stage cross-check: Grokipedia/Wikipedia 'Carbohydrate', 'Glycogen', 'Carbohydrate loading', 'Ketosis'. Grokipedia WebFetch 403 this session.
framing_note: Reveal the MECHANISM (quick fuel + storage battery). Scene-led (a candy rush; a marathoner's pasta dinner; hitting the wall at mile 20), never 'What is a carbohydrate?'. Accuracy rail: do NOT claim carbs are strictly essential — the body can run on fat/ketones (nod to it so the low-carb view isn't strawmanned), so frame carbs as the READY/DEFAULT fuel; brain-runs-on-glucose (~120 g/day) taught as concept, never the number as the answer; glycogen taught as 'the carb battery', not biochem. Dinner-test payoff = the glycogen-battery / carb-loading rung. Settled mechanism, but keep the low-carb steel-man alive in the fruit/ketone rungs.

name: Whole vs refined grain: what's hidden in the bran
strand: Macros: why your body needs them
scope: A grain of wheat or rice has three parts, and refining throws two of them away. T1: a whole grain has a fibrous outer BRAN, a nutrient-packed GERM (the baby-plant embryo), and a big starchy ENDOSPERM (the energy store) — brown rice and whole-wheat flour keep all three. T2 (payoff): milling to make WHITE rice or WHITE flour strips off the bran and germ, leaving mostly the starchy endosperm — whiter, fluffier, longer-lasting on the shelf, but with the fiber and most nutrients removed. T3: history's hard lesson — when late-1800s mills began polishing rice bright white, whole regions of Asia came down with beriberi, a nerve-and-heart disease, because the vital nutrient lived in the discarded bran; switching back to unpolished rice cured it. T4: that's why white flour and rice are now 'enriched' — a few vitamins are sprayed back in to replace what milling removed, though the fiber never returns. T5: stone-ground and sourdough whole-grain breads keep more of the intact grain — part of why a dense traditional loaf eats so differently from a fluffy white supermarket one.
source: Search: beriberi (Wikipedia 'Thiamine deficiency'; Nobelprize.org Eijkman; ScienceDirect 'Christiaan Eijkman') confirming polished/white rice removes the thiamine-rich bran, late-19th-c. milling change, Takaki (1880s Japanese Navy) and Eijkman (1897) work, cure via unpolished rice, and modern enrichment. Bran/germ/endosperm anatomy and refining trade-offs are established food science (build-stage cross-check: Grokipedia/Wikipedia 'Whole grain', 'Bran', 'Cereal germ').
framing_note: Traditional-foods lean fits (whole grain vs stripped-white). Reveal the MECHANISM (bran/germ/endosperm; milling discards the good parts). Scene-led (brown vs white rice; a sack of white flour; a navy/village falling ill). Accuracy rail: beriberi = thiamine (B1) deficiency from POLISHED rice, late-1800s milling era — teach the STORY (the nutrient was in the discarded bran; unpolished rice cured it), never 'thiamine' or a scientist's name as the tested answer; enrichment adds some vitamins back but NOT fiber. Dinner-test payoff = the white-rice / beriberi rung. Settled.

name: Pemmican: the fat-and-protein food with no carbs
strand: Macros: why your body needs them
scope: The original survival superfood proves fat + protein alone can power a body for months. T1: pemmican is dried meat pounded to a powder and mixed roughly half-and-half with rendered fat (sometimes studded with dried berries) — a dense, nearly indestructible food developed by the Plains peoples of North America. T2 (payoff): it's almost pure FAT and PROTEIN with essentially no carbs, yet fur-trade voyageurs and polar explorers lived and hauled loaded canoes on roughly a pound of it a day — living proof the body runs fine on fat-and-protein when it must. T3: because it's so dry and fat-sealed, pemmican keeps for years with no refrigeration — the reason it crossed oceans on expeditions long before the canned tin existed.
source: Search: pemmican (Wikipedia 'Pemmican'; Britannica 'Pemmican'; Lewis & Clark 'Making Pemmican') confirming ~1:1 dried-meat-to-rendered-fat, optional dried berries, Cree 'pimihkan' = 'manufactured fat', Plains-peoples origin, voyageur/polar-expedition use ~1 lb/day, multi-year shelf stability.
framing_note: Food-driven history where the FOOD is the anchor (Cree 'pimihkan' = manufactured fat). Reveal the amazing FACT: a carb-free food fueling extreme labor. Scene-led (a voyageur's daily ration; a polar sledge), never 'What is pemmican?'. Prep-frame fine (you pound, you render). Accuracy rail: Indigenous North American origin (Plains / Cree) — attribute correctly, never as a European invention; berries are optional and the only carb source. Keep butchery/rendering matter-of-fact, not gory. Dinner-test payoff = the no-carbs-yet-fueled-explorers rung. Ties the whole strand together (a food that IS the macros, stripped to two).
